subject: Science
chapter: Chapter 12: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
central_question: How does electric current produce magnetic fields and forces, and how are these ideas applied to electromagnets and safe domestic electric circuits?
in_scope_units: Oersted's observation linking electric current and magnetism.
Magnetic field and magnetic field lines around a bar magnet.
Magnetic field due to a current-carrying straight conductor and the right-hand thumb rule.
Magnetic field due to a current-carrying circular loop.
Magnetic field due to a solenoid and formation of an electromagnet.
Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field and Fleming's left-hand rule.
Domestic electric circuits: live, neutral and earth wires, parallel connection, fuses, short-circuiting and overloading.
banned_topics: Detailed derivation of Ohm's law, electrical power and Joule heating calculations from the Electricity chapter, except where a fuse is discussed for safety.
Detailed construction and working of electric motors and generators, which are only named in this chapter extract.
Electromagnetic induction and transformer theory beyond the content provided.

known_pitfalls.claim: Magnetic field lines start at the north pole and end permanently at the south pole.
known_pitfalls.correction: Outside a magnet they go from north to south, but inside the magnet they return from south to north, so magnetic field lines are closed curves.

known_pitfalls.claim: Two magnetic field lines can cross if the field is strong.
known_pitfalls.correction: Field lines never cross because the magnetic field at one point cannot have two directions.

known_pitfalls.claim: Increasing distance from a current-carrying straight wire increases its magnetic field.
known_pitfalls.correction: For the same current, the field becomes weaker as distance from the wire increases.

known_pitfalls.claim: The right-hand thumb rule gives the direction of force on a conductor.
known_pitfalls.correction: The right-hand thumb rule gives magnetic field direction around a current-carrying conductor; Fleming's left-hand rule gives the force direction.

known_pitfalls.claim: The green-insulated wire is the live wire.
known_pitfalls.correction: In the chapter, the green-insulated wire is the earth wire; the live wire is usually red and the neutral wire black.

known_pitfalls.claim: Short-circuiting means current becomes very small.
known_pitfalls.correction: When live and neutral wires come into direct contact, current increases abruptly and heavily.

recommended_example_progression: Use NCERT Activities 12.1-12.3 to establish the magnetic effect of current and properties of field lines.
Use NCERT Activities 12.4-12.5 and Example 12.1 for field direction around a straight conductor.
Use NCERT Activity 12.6 and the solenoid section for circular coils, uniform fields and electromagnets.
Use NCERT Activity 12.7 and Example 12.2 for force direction and Fleming's left-hand rule.
Use the domestic-circuit in-text questions and end Exercises Q2, Q8 and Q9 for short circuits, earthing and fuse safety.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The end-of-chapter EXERCISES contain Questions 1-9 on field patterns, direction rules, force, short circuits and earthing.
